Cost guide

What does an event planner cost in Australia?

Published Australian figures disagree with each other by thousands of dollars. They are not wrong, they are measuring different things. This guide puts the numbers side by side, explains the gap, and shows where a planning fee sits in a real wedding budget breakdown.

Get event planning quotesCompare planning services
  • Sources named and dated
  • Australian figures only
  • Updated September 2026

The short answer

A planning fee in Australia usually lands somewhere between $1,500 and $6,000 for most private events, with two things pushing it higher: a percentage-of-budget fee on a large event, and a full-service scope on a wedding with many suppliers. On-the-day coordination sits at the bottom of that range. Full planning sits at the top of it or above.

That is a wide answer, and the width is the point. There is no rate card for event planning in Australia, because a planning fee prices scope and time rather than a product. The rest of this guide is about how to tell which number applies to you.

The published figures

What the Australian sources actually say

Three Australian sources are cited more than any others for this question. Here is what each one publishes, with its date, so you can see where they agree and where they do not.

Australian planner and coordinator pricing as published by three named sources. These are third-party figures collected in September 2026, not a quote for your event.
SourceWhat it coversPublished figures
Easy Weddings, guide updated February 2026, drawing on its 2025 Wedding Industry ReportWeddings, Australia-wideDay-of coordinator roughly $1,500 to $2,000. Full-service planning $5,000 to $6,000. Hourly consultations $75 to $100. Average Australian wedding budget $35,315, which puts a $6,000 planning fee at about 17 per cent of the total.
Airtasker Australia, cost guide updated February 2025Weddings, Australia-wide plus city mediansOverall $1,000 to $20,000 with a median around $8,000. Commonly 10 to 15 per cent of total wedding budget. Hourly $70 to $120. Day-of coordination $1,000 to $5,000. Estimates 200 to 300 hours of work per wedding. City medians include Sydney $4,200 to $4,500, Melbourne $1,800 to $2,200, Brisbane $1,600 to $1,800 and Perth $1,600 to $1,800.
FAME Events, Australian event agency, September 2024Events other than weddingsPlanning for a straightforward event typically starts around $5,000, covering the planning fee only and not the event budget. A percentage model of 15 to 20 per cent is described as the less common approach.

Scroll the table sideways to see every column.

The gap

Why the published ranges disagree

Easy Weddings says $5,000 to $6,000 for full service. Airtasker's median is $8,000 with city medians under $4,500. Both are describing the same market. Four things explain the gap.

They are measuring different scopes

A marketplace median mixes coordination jobs, partial planning and full planning into one number. A wedding publication quoting full service is describing one specific package. The median of a mixed set will always sit below the top of a single scope.

Flat fee and percentage fee diverge as budgets grow

At the $35,315 average Australian wedding budget, a 12 per cent fee is about $4,200, which sits inside both published ranges. At a $90,000 budget the same percentage is about $10,800, which sits inside Airtasker's range and well outside Easy Weddings'. Same planner, same method, very different number.

City medians reflect what is commonly bought there

Airtasker's Sydney median of $4,200 to $4,500 sits far above its Brisbane and Perth medians of $1,600 to $1,800. That is not only a cost-of-living difference. It reflects a different mix of jobs being booked in each market.

Hourly rates hide the hours

Airtasker quotes $70 to $120 per hour and separately estimates 200 to 300 hours to plan one wedding. Multiply those out and the hourly figure stops looking cheap. Almost nobody buys wedding planning by the hour for this reason.

By level

What each level of help typically costs

On-the-day coordination

The cheapest and most commonly bought planning product in Australia. Published ranges are $1,500 to $2,000 (Easy Weddings) and $1,000 to $5,000 (Airtasker).

What moves it: handover length, one site or two, guest count.

  • Handover four to six weeks out
  • Every supplier confirmed and briefed
  • Run sheet written and circulated
  • On-site management for the day
  • Your plan and suppliers unchanged

Partial planning

Sits between the two published poles and is the least standardised product, because what is left to do varies enormously between couples.

What moves it: how many suppliers remain, and how late you start.

  • Supplier shortlists for what is unbooked
  • Timeline and budget management
  • Styling refined against what exists
  • Coordination on the day
  • You keep the decisions you care about

Full planning

Easy Weddings publishes $5,000 to $6,000. Percentage-based quotes at 10 to 15 per cent will exceed that on any budget above roughly $45,000.

What moves it: total budget, supplier count, dry hire venue, travel.

  • Concept and styling direction
  • Venue shortlisting and contract review
  • Every supplier sourced and booked
  • Budget held in one place
  • Full run sheet and day management

Budget breakdown

Where the planning fee sits in a wedding budget breakdown

Against the $35,315 average Australian wedding budget published by Easy Weddings, here is what a planning fee looks like next to everything else.

Illustrative wedding budget breakdown against the $35,315 Australian average published by Easy Weddings. Percentages are a planning aid, not a market survey. Your split will differ, particularly if your venue is dry hire.
LineShare of budgetOn a $35,315 budget
Venue and catering40 to 50 per cent$14,000 to $17,700
Photography and video10 to 12 per cent$3,500 to $4,200
Attire, rings and beauty8 to 12 per cent$2,800 to $4,200
Flowers and styling8 to 12 per cent$2,800 to $4,200
Entertainment and AV5 to 8 per cent$1,800 to $2,800
Planning or coordination5 to 17 per cent$1,750 to $6,000
Stationery, cake and transport4 to 6 per cent$1,400 to $2,100
Contingency5 to 10 per cent$1,750 to $3,500

Scroll the table sideways to see every column.

Two things are worth noticing in that breakdown. The first is that the planning line has by far the widest range of anything on the list, because it is the only line where you choose how much of the product to buy. The second is the contingency line, which people delete first and regret most. Suppliers do not go over budget. Decisions made late do.

If you are building your own event budget template, use this order of operations: set the total, set the guest count, allocate venue and catering first because it is the largest and the least flexible, then work down. Put the contingency in at the start rather than hoping for it at the end.

Non-weddings

What planning costs for events that are not weddings

There is far less published Australian benchmark data outside weddings, and what exists is structured differently.

The clearest Australian reference point is FAME Events, an Australian event agency, which published in September 2024 that planning for a straightforward event typically starts around $5,000, and that a percentage model of 15 to 20 per cent is used but less often. Critically, that figure is the planning fee only. It does not include the venue, catering, suppliers or anything else the event actually costs.

What tends to be cheaper than a wedding

Kids parties, small private functions and single-session corporate events. Fewer suppliers, shorter timelines, and often a single venue handling catering and staffing in one contract. Many planners quote these as a fixed package because the scope is predictable.

What tends to be dearer than a wedding

Conferences, awards nights and multi-day programmes. The planning work is heavier even where the styling is lighter, because there are sessions to schedule, speakers to manage, AV to specify, run sheets to circulate to internal stakeholders and an approval process to satisfy.

The dry hire multiplier

Whatever the occasion, a dry hire venue is the single biggest scope multiplier there is. A packaged venue supplies the room, the staff, the kitchen, the tables, the chairs, the glassware and the liquor licence. A dry hire venue supplies the room. Everything else has to be sourced, delivered, installed, staffed and removed, which is a different quantity of planning work entirely, and it is the most common reason two apparently similar events are quoted thousands apart.

What is not in the fee

What a planning fee does not cover

The most expensive misunderstanding in this whole subject is confusing the planning fee with the event budget. They are separate pools of money and they are not close in size.

Your planning fee pays for a person's time, expertise and supplier network. Your event budget pays for the venue, the catering, the drinks, the photographer, the flowers, the cake, the hire items, the entertainment and everything else that physically happens. FAME Events makes this point directly in its Australian pricing guidance: the figure it quotes is the planning fee only.

On the $35,315 average Australian wedding budget published by Easy Weddings, a $5,000 planning fee is around 14 per cent of the total, and the remaining $30,000 or so still has to buy the event. When someone says a planner cost them $6,000, they almost always mean the fee. When someone says their wedding cost $6,000, they mean something else entirely.

Things that sit outside almost every planning fee

  • Supplier costs. Everything the planner books on your behalf is invoiced by that supplier, usually to you directly.
  • Travel beyond a set radius. Most planners define a service area and charge travel outside it. For a regional or interstate event this can include accommodation.
  • Additional site visits and meetings. Packages usually include a set number. Extra ones are billed.
  • Extra on-site staff. A large guest count or a two-site day often needs a second coordinator, quoted separately.
  • Styling hire. Design direction is planning work. The physical items are a hire cost from a hire company.
  • Overtime. If the event runs long, the on-site team is usually billed by the hour past the contracted finish.

Value

When a planner saves you money, and when they do not

A planner is not automatically a net cost. On some events the fee is genuinely offset. On others it is not, and it is worth being honest about which is which.

Where the fee is often offset

On a dry hire venue, where a planner who has built there before knows what the site actually needs and stops you hiring the wrong quantity of everything. On a large guest count, where per head decisions compound and a five dollar error is a thousand dollar error. On a compressed timeline, where paying a supplier a rush premium is the alternative. And on any event where the budget is large enough that a planner negotiating supplier contracts recovers a meaningful share of their own fee.

Where the fee is a genuine additional cost

On a small event at a packaged venue with a short supplier list. If you are having 40 guests at a restaurant that handles food, drinks, staff and the room, there is not much left for a planner to optimise, and the fee is what it is. That is not an argument against hiring one. It is an argument for buying coordination rather than full planning, so that you are paying for the part you actually need.

The honest test

Count the suppliers you will have to manage. Under about five, at a venue that handles catering and staffing, you probably need coordination rather than planning. Over about ten, or at a dry hire site, the planning fee starts doing real work.

What you are really buying

Most people who hire a planner do not do it to save money. They do it to stop being the switchboard for twelve suppliers while also being the host. That is a legitimate thing to buy and it does not need a financial justification.

Comparing quotes

How to compare two planner quotes properly

Most people compare the headline figure. The headline figure is the least informative part of a planning quote.

01

Line up the scope, not the price

Put the two inclusion lists next to each other before you look at either number. A quote that is $3,000 cheaper is very often a partial planning package sitting next to a full one.

02

Find the exclusions

Travel outside a set radius, extra site visits, meetings past a set number, styling hire and additional on-site staff are the five things most often excluded. Ask for them in writing.

03

Check the fee model

A flat fee is fixed. A percentage fee rises with your budget, which means the quote you accept in month one is not the fee you pay in month nine if the budget grows.

04

Ask who is on site

Some planners run your event personally. Others send a coordinator from their team. Both are legitimate. Only one of them is what you thought you were buying.

Straight answers

Cost questions, answered

How much does a wedding planner cost in Australia?

Easy Weddings, in a guide updated February 2026, publishes $5,000 to $6,000 for full-service wedding planning and roughly $1,500 to $2,000 for a day-of coordinator. Airtasker's Australian cost guide, updated February 2025, gives a wider $1,000 to $20,000 range with a median around $8,000, and notes that planners commonly charge 10 to 15 per cent of the total wedding budget. The difference between those figures is scope, not error.

What percentage of a wedding budget goes to a planner?

Airtasker reports 10 to 15 per cent as the common percentage-based model in Australia. Easy Weddings observes that a $6,000 planning fee is about 17 per cent of the $35,315 average Australian wedding budget. So a planning line of roughly 10 to 17 per cent is normal for full planning, and considerably less if you are buying coordination only.

Is a percentage fee or a flat fee better?

A flat fee is more predictable and suits a budget you expect to hold. A percentage fee suits a large or uncertain budget because it scales with the work, but it also means the fee grows if the event does. If you take a percentage quote, ask what the percentage is calculated on and whether there is a floor.

How much does on-the-day coordination cost?

Published Australian ranges are roughly $1,500 to $2,000 according to Easy Weddings, updated February 2026, and $1,000 to $5,000 according to Airtasker, updated February 2025. What moves it most is how long the handover period is, whether the ceremony and reception are at the same site, and how many people the coordinator needs on the ground.

Why is a Sydney planner more expensive than a Perth one?

Airtasker's Australian city medians show Sydney at $4,200 to $4,500 against Brisbane and Perth at $1,600 to $1,800. Part of that is cost base. A larger part is what people in each market typically buy, since a median mixes coordination jobs and full planning jobs together in different proportions.

Do I pay Plan Your Event anything?

No. Enquiring through Plan Your Event is free and there is no obligation to book. You engage and pay your planner directly, and the planning fees discussed on this page are the planner's fees, not ours.
